Forget 10,000 Followers. Find Your First 100 People Who Actually Care.

Playbooklowob research

By Chris WellsFrom lowob RESEARCH · 12 June 2026 · 7-minute read · Growth

The first meaningful community milestone is not 10,000 followers, 5,000 Discord members or a trending announcement. It is 100 people who understand why the project matters and repeatedly choose to participate. Our piece The first hundred covers recruiting them; this one covers running them: what counts as caring, the one ritual to start with, the roles to give, the weekly review and when to grow.

A hundred is small enough for a team to know many members directly and large enough for useful patterns, peer relationships and early culture to emerge. It forces the company to learn why people return before paying to acquire thousands who do not. This is the operating stage of our guide to building a community that lasts.

Define "cares" as behaviour

Do not define an active member as someone who joined a server or reacted to an announcement. For the first 100, require one or more meaningful behaviours:

BehaviourWhat it showsHow to record it
Attended two sessionsReturning, not samplingAttendance list
Answered another member's questionPeer value existsThread or channel log
Tested the product and gave useful feedbackProduct contributionFeedback tracker
Created a resource, integration or piece of contentBuilding on the projectResource list
Introduced a relevant participantWillingness to vouchReferral log
Returned in multiple weeksHabitWeekly activity
Completed an economically or commercially valuable actionValue to the businessProduct or CRM data

The definition should reflect what makes the product or network stronger. Platform metrics can help but do not replace it. Discord's Server Insights separates "visitors", members who open a channel, from "communicators", members who post, and tracks new member retention as the share of new members who return after a week. Discord suggests about 30% communicators as a healthy goal. Those figures describe presence. The table above describes contribution.

Recruit from a narrow shared problem

Broad communities struggle because members have little reason to recognise one another. "People interested in Web3" is not a useful initial group. "Treasury leaders at crypto companies evaluating stablecoin yield and counterparty risk" is. Narrowness increases the probability that one member's question is valuable to another.

Begin with a member thesis:

We are assembling [specific people] who are actively trying to [specific outcome] and can help one another by [specific exchange].

This is more compelling than asking strangers to join a company server. The founding team should recruit the first 25 to 40 members through direct relationships and high-context outreach, using the loop described in The first hundred. The invitation should explain why that person specifically belongs, who else will participate and what the first experience will deliver. Exclusivity without relevance is vanity. Relevance creates the feeling of being in the right room.

Start with one recurring ritual

Do not launch with twenty empty channels. Launch with one repeatable reason to gather: a weekly product teardown, a private market-signal briefing, a founder problem-solving session, an integration clinic for developers, a rotating member case study or a research exchange around a narrow market.

The ritual should make members useful to one another, and the first test is whether newcomers get a response. Kraut and colleagues' study of Usenet groups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day. By day 30, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still participating, against 12% of those who got none. Replies from established members and replies using inclusive "we" language were linked to longer stays. Kraut and Resnick's Building Successful Online Communities (MIT Press) turns findings like these into design claims about contribution and commitment. A ritual with a host who makes sure every first question gets answered is that research put into practice.

Collect the best questions, decisions and resources from each session, then return them to the group as a growing knowledge base. Our piece on Discord and Telegram strategy covers how to stop that knowledge disappearing into chat.

Do not ask how to make a community look large. Ask what would make 100 specific people return without being chased.

Give members consequential roles

Early members should be able to influence something real. They might test a feature, shape documentation, help select speakers, lead a working group, nominate future members or contribute to a public guide. The role must have a visible effect. Decorative councils and meaningless badges teach people that participation is theatre.

Recognition should follow contribution. Highlight the member who solved a difficult problem, introduced two collaborators or produced a resource, not merely the person who posted most often. Nielsen's work on participation inequality makes the same warning: rewarding raw activity lets the most prolific few dominate, so promote quality contributions instead.

Run a weekly member-health review

For every member, track:

  • Source of introduction
  • Reason for joining
  • First meaningful action
  • Relationships formed
  • Contributions made
  • Last meaningful participation
  • Likely next role

Each week, identify five members who need a better introduction, a clearer invitation or a direct conversation. Early community operations are closer to relationship management than mass social media. Our piece on community management versus social media management explains why the person running this review should be a host, not a publisher.

Illustrative example: one ritual, one review
Decision
A B2B data infrastructure company replaced a 14-channel public server with a fortnightly integration clinic for 40 invited engineers and a weekly member-health review.
Reason and owner
Most channels were silent and support questions were going unanswered. The developer-relations lead owned the clinic and the review.
What changed
Each clinic ended with notes returned to members. After two months, members were answering most clinic follow-up questions themselves, and the next cohort was invited from their introductions.

Illustrative: a composite of developer-community patterns, not a single company.

Grow through member density

Invite the next cohort only when the first group is receiving consistent value. Ask active members whom they know with the same problem and what expertise is missing from the room.

This creates density: a higher probability that any member can find a relevant conversation, collaborator or answer. Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities (vendor research) found average engagement rates of 2% to 12% across surfaces, with smaller communities engaging at higher rates and real-time chat declining fastest as communities grew. Density matters more than raw size because it produces the experiences people describe to others. In-person sessions can raise it further; events that pay back covers how to judge whether they do.

The first 100 members establish norms the next 1,000 will inherit. If the initial culture rewards speculation, extraction and staff dependence, scale will amplify those behaviours. If it rewards useful contribution, informed disagreement and peer support, growth has something worth multiplying.

lowob takeaways

  • Define caring as behaviour. Count answers, tests, resources and returns, not joins and reactions.
  • Keep the group narrow. A shared, specific problem makes members useful to one another.
  • Answer every first question. Newcomers who get replies are far more likely to stay.
  • Set the norms early. The first 100 establish what the next 1,000 will inherit.

Common questions

How do you build a community from zero?

Write a narrow member thesis, recruit the first 25 to 40 people personally, start one recurring ritual that makes members useful to each other and grow only when that group gets consistent value.

What counts as an active community member?

Someone who does something that makes the network stronger: answers a question, tests the product, creates a resource, introduces a relevant person or returns over several weeks. Joining or reacting does not count.

How do you keep new community members engaged?

Make sure their first contribution gets a response. Research on online groups found newcomers whose first post drew several replies were more than twice as likely to still be active a month later.

When should a small community start growing?

When the first group is receiving consistent value. Ask active members who they know with the same problem and what expertise is missing, and invite the next cohort from those answers.

Sources and notes

  • Kraut, Wang, Butler, Joyce and Burke, Beyond Information: Developing the Relationship between the Individual and the Group in Online Communities, manuscript dated 18 April 2008. Working paper; Usenet groups; behavioural measures only.
  • Kraut and Resnick, Building Successful Online Communities: Evidence-Based Social Design, MIT Press, paperback edition February 2016. Academic book; design claims drawn from social science research.
  • Discord, Getting to Know Your Server With Server Insights, undated. Platform documentation; the 30% communicator goal is Discord's guidance, not a research finding.
  • Common Room, 360: Community-Led Growth Report, 17 November 2022. Vendor research on 141 communities using Common Room.
  • Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule, 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis.
  • The behaviour table, review fields and example are lowob's framework and illustration.

Next move

Write your member thesis in one sentence, then pick the one ritual you will run every week for the next two months. Before the first session, decide who will make sure every newcomer's question gets an answer.
